resolved.title: *args 参数
resolved.description:
[s0l0!-header][h1]*args[/h1][/s0l0!-header] 

Python allows you to have functions with [b]varying numbers of arguments[/b].
Using [b]*args[/b] as a function parameter enables you to pass an arbitrary number of arguments to that function. The arguments are then accessible as the tuple [b]args [/b]in the body of the function.

[s0l0!-header][b]Example:[/b][/s0l0!-header][code format="py" codeId="443"]def function(named_arg, [b]*args[/b]):
   print(named_arg)
   print(args)

function(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)[/code]
[note]The parameter [b]*args[/b] must come after the named parameters to a function.
The name [b]args [/b]is just a convention; you can choose to use another.[/note]

resolved.title: **kwargs
resolved.description:
[s0l0!-header][h1]**kwargs[/h1][/s0l0!-header] 

[b]**kwargs [/b](standing for keyword arguments) allows you to handle named arguments that you have not defined in advance.
The keyword arguments return a [b]dictionary[/b] in which the keys are the argument names, and the values are the argument values.

[s0l0!-header][b]Example:[/b][/s0l0!-header][code format="py" codeId="445"]def my_func(x, y=7, *args, [b]**kwargs[/b]):
   print(kwargs)

my_func(2, 3, 4, 5, 6, a=7, b=8)[/code]
[b]a[/b] and [b]b[/b] are the names of the arguments that we passed to the function call.
[note]The arguments returned by [b]**kwargs[/b] are not included in [b]*args[/b].[/note]
